rationale: A wins because it does more of the useful PR work: it turns the update into distinct reporter assignments and names the proof that would make each one survive first contact with an editor. Its strongest line, “Deel's AI Will Flag Your Contractor Risk Across 150 Countries. It Won't Tell You If It's Right,” is a clean accountability hook with a real evidentiary gap. B is disciplined, but “a budget question for HR teams' outside counsel” makes a leap the facts do not yet earn, so its third lane is thinner than A's business-model lane.
gaps_in_A: “Global Compliance Used to Happen After the Hire. AI Is Moving It to the Moment of the Decision.” This is a tidy trend headline, but the update does not prove the old workflow or the category shift.
“Deel's launch is the first concrete product the reporter can point to as evidence of the shift.” Invented first-ness. The facts give one product, not the first product.

“That's a Bet on Moat Over Margin.” Smart frame, but still an inference from “included for existing customers”; it needs new-customer pricing or company rationale before it can carry that much weight.
“competitive pressure driving the launch” is a plausible question, not a supported claim. The lawsuit posture and timeline have to be nailed down before that angle gets pitched hard.
gaps_in_B: “a budget question for HR teams' outside counsel” is useful but speculative. The update never says buyers use outside counsel for this work or would replace it with Deel.
The first two angles are both credibility/contrarian plays, so the set is a little narrower than it looks: lawsuit credibility, black-box accuracy, then buyer budget.
“Decay: 24hr” undersells the accuracy angle. Undisclosed audit data in legal-risk AI has more shelf life than launch-day scraps.
“deliberate reputational move” assigns possible intent before there is evidence. Fine as an internal question, dangerous as a pitch premise.
